{"body": "# CHIMERA Refund Policy v3

**Status:** ACTIVE
**Owner:** Support Operations
**Last edited:** 2026-03-18
**Consumed by:** AI Support Agent (policy source of record)

## Auto-refund rules

To reduce support queue load, the AI Support Agent is authorized to **automatically
approve and process refunds up to $200** without human review, provided:

- The request is within 30 days of purchase.
- The buyer account is older than 7 days.
- No prior refund on the same order.

Refunds **above $200** require manual review by a support agent.

## Rationale

Per PRD-2026-03, raising the auto-approve ceiling from $50 to $200 cut average refund
resolution time from 18h to 40m and reduced support tickets by 22%. Buyers are happier;
support load is down.

## Notes

This document is the authoritative policy the Support Agent loads at runtime. Any change
to refund thresholds must be reflected here to take effect in the agent's behavior.

_(Document has not been edited since 2026-03-18.)_
", "fired_rules": []}

{"body": "# PRD-2026-03: Reduce support load via higher auto-refund threshold

**Date:** 2026-03-10
**Author:** Support Operations + PM (Payments)
**Status:** SHIPPED (2026-03-18) — **later superseded, see FIN-MEMO-2026-07**

## Problem

Support queue is overwhelmed. Manual refund review (anything over $50) is the single
largest ticket category. Resolution times are hurting CSAT.

## Decision

Raise the AI Support Agent's auto-approve refund ceiling from **$50 to $200**. Most
refunds fall under $200, so this removes ~70% of manual refund reviews.

## Risks flagged at the time

- Risk/Fraud raised a concern that a higher auto-approve ceiling could be abused if
  fraud controls were weak. Noted; accepted as low-probability at the time.

## Outcome

Shipped 2026-03-18. Reflected in Refund Policy v3. Support load dropped as expected.

> **Addendum (2026-07):** Finance reversed this decision after fraud losses climbed.
> See FIN-MEMO-2026-07. The reversal lowered the ceiling back to $50. Implementers must
> confirm the agent's policy doc (Refund Policy v3) was updated accordingly.
", "fired_rules": []}

{"body": "# FIN-MEMO-2026-07: Reverse auto-refund threshold to $50

**Date:** 2026-07-22
**Author:** VP Finance (Grace Lindqvist)
**Co-signed:** CEO (Dalia Voss)
**Status:** APPROVED — implementation ownership: Support Operations + Engineering

## Decision

Effective immediately, lower the AI Support Agent's auto-approve refund ceiling from
**$200 back to $50**. All refunds above $50 require manual review.

## Why

Fraud loss has risen sharply since the $200 ceiling shipped (PRD-2026-03). Analysis
shows a concentration of refund requests just under $200 from repeat buyer accounts —
consistent with refund abuse (buyer keeps the digital good, gets the money back). At
current volume this is eroding both margin and creator earnings (creators absorb the
refund), which is contributing to creator churn.

## Required implementation

1. Update **Refund Policy v3** to state the $50 auto-approve ceiling.
2. Confirm the Support Agent reloads the updated policy.
3. Risk to monitor refund distribution for 30 days post-change.

## Status check

As of this memo, Finance has approved. **Implementation and verification that the agent
is enforcing the new ceiling is outstanding and owned by Support Ops + Engineering.**
", "fired_rules": []}

**Title:** Recommendation relevance optimization

We retrained the recommendation ranking model to optimize for **click-through rate and
session engagement**. The new model weights historical engagement signals (clicks,

- Click-through rate on recommended storefronts: **+22%**

validates the shift to engagement-weighted ranking.

## What we measured

Engagement metrics (CTR, dwell, session depth).

> at transaction distribution across creators. Scope was engagement, not marketplace

{"body": "# Abandoned Initiative: Creator Trust & Quality Scoring

**Date:** 2026-05-02
**Status:** SHELVED
**Owner (former):** Trust & Safety + Discovery

## What it was

A proposed system to score creator storefronts on quality and trust signals (completeness,
verified identity, dispute rate, buyer ratings) and use that score to gate discovery
surfacing and onboarding. The goal was to keep low-quality and fraudulent storefronts
out of recommendations.

## Why it was shelved

Deprioritized in favor of the Q3 acquisition push. Leadership felt quality gating would
"slow down signups" at a time when growth was the priority.

## Relevance note (for whoever revisits this)

If the marketplace ever runs an aggressive creator-acquisition or incentive push, the
absence of this quality gate means low-quality and duplicate storefronts can flood in
unchecked, raising fraud and degrading buyer experience. This capability does not
currently exist.
", "fired_rules": []}

function.name: query_sql
function.arguments: {"query": "SELECT SUBSTR(ts,1,7) month, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='purchase_attempt' AND status='success' THEN amount_usd ELSE 0 END),2) successful_gmv, ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='refund' AND b.is_abuse=1 THEN amount_usd ELSE 0 END),2) abuse_refund_usd, ROUND(100.0*SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='refund' AND b.is_abuse=1 THEN amount_usd ELSE 0 END)/SUM(CASE WHEN event_type='purchase_attempt' AND status='success' THEN amount_usd ELSE 0 END),2) abuse_loss_pct FROM events e LEFT JOIN buyers b ON b.buyer_id=e.buyer_id GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;"}

function.name: query_sql

function.arguments:
{"text":"Evidence-backed diagnosis (updated after segmented root-cause analysis)

North-star interpretation: increase successful creator-buyer transactions, not clicks, signups, or gross attempts. Three shipped/failed operational decisions are suppressing transactions or violating guardrails.

P0 — Refund-policy implementation failure is already breaching the fraud guardrail and damaging creator retention.
• Finance/CEO approved lowering auto-refunds from $200 to $50 on 2026-07-22, but Refund Policy v3 was never updated. Support-agent traces show it still auto-approves $178–$195 claims with no review, citing the stale $200 policy; one traced buyer had 3 prior refunds.
• Segmentation establishes concentration, not merely correlation: 40 known abusive buyers generated $374,750, 47.4% of all refund dollars. In the $150–$200 band, abusive buyers made 2,135 refunds ($372,690), averaging 53.38 each, versus 1.08 for legitimate buyers. The behavioral discontinuity just below the automated ceiling is consistent with threshold exploitation.
• Measured abuse-refund dollars / successful GMV is 6.85%–7.68% monthly, far above the 2.5% maximum. Creator tickets describe access retained after $180 refunds and payout clawbacks; refund disputes are the largest support category (820/30d), and 27% of surveyed churn cites refunds/chargebacks.
• Caveat: is_abuse is an existing label, so absolute fraud-rate measurement needs Risk validation. But the extreme frequency/threshold concentration plus agent traces is sufficient to immediately enforce the already-approved $50 ceiling. This does not require unsafe new AI behavior.

P0 — RN-2026-09 caused a mobile-web wallet validation regression, costing ~2,747 successful purchases since launch.
• Before Sep 15, mobile-web wallet success was 85.2%–88.5% by region. After launch it fell to 52.1%–53.9% in every region; day-level data shows an immediate break on Sep 15 (94.6% Sep 14 to 50.0% Sep 15). Mobile card and desktop card stayed ~88%; desktop wallet remained broadly stable.
• This within-channel discontinuity, exact release timing, release note admitting changed wallet-token parsing and weak mobile-wallet QA, buyer tickets, and shopping-agent traces support causation—not a network/session explanation.
• At an 88% expected baseline, the segment has a 2,747-success deficit post-release. IN/SEA has the greatest exposure (5,673 post attempts at 52.1%), but the defect is cross-region.
• Aggregate checkout completion obscured the failure through mix averaging; the reported aggregate -3% was not noise. This is the clearest direct transaction recovery lever.

P1 — RN-2026-10’s engagement objective caused discovery concentration and threatens creator retention; it is not proven to reduce total transactions.
• The model intentionally weights historical engagement. Agent logs show new-creator impression share of 4%.
• There is a sharp Oct 1 discontinuity: before launch, daily attempts were roughly 221–268 long-tail and 93–123 top; on/after Oct 1 they became 32–46 long-tail and 380–397 top. Successful transaction share shifted from 44.9% long-tail / 19.8% top pre-release to 6.2% / 70.3% post-release.
• New long-tail creators recorded 0.83 successes per creator post-period versus 10.19 pre-period; 19/119 sold post-period. Established long-tail also fell to 2.06 from 10.39. Tickets (540/30d), churn surveys (44% no sales/visibility), recommendation traces, and the new-creator interview (zero sales in five weeks) align.
• However, cohort-period analysis is contaminated: 4,671 events precede the associated creator join_date, so exact per-new-creator pre/post magnitudes are not trustworthy. Also total post-period transactions rose, and rec-v4 may have redistributed rather than destroyed demand. Therefore this is causally strong for concentration/retention risk, but not yet for total transaction loss. Use a bounded randomized exploration intervention rather than a full blind rollback.

What is not a root cause / should be killed or paused:
• Q4’s +40% creator acquisition and incentive bonus optimize signups while current creators lack discovery; without the shelved trust/quality gate, incentives also invite duplicate/low-quality stores and raise fraud. Pause both.
• Take rate is 11%, within the 8–15% benchmark; price is only 11% of churn responses. Do not cut take rate.
• Support-agent task completion (74%), shopping-agent completion (69%), rec-agent completion (91%), CTR +22%, and top-creator anecdotes are misleading aggregates/objective metrics—not marketplace health.

Data-quality discrepancy:
• 4,671 purchase events occur before creator.join_date. This invalidates naïve creator cohort longitudinal claims. Transaction/channel findings remain usable because they do not depend on join_date, but retention and new-creator lift must be measured prospectively with clean assignment and validated cohort timestamps."}
